title: Conditional probability as a fraction
summary: P(A | B) as a share of the people (or emails) where B happened, on a 1,000-email spam table.

blocks.title: How many emails contain free?

define.meaning: Something that happens or not, such as “the email is spam” or “it contains free”.
The share of the whole table where $A$ is true.

blocks.why: A conditional probability only looks at part of the table. First find the part.
blocks.prompt: 1,000 emails: 200 are spam, 800 are not (ham). The word “free” appears in 120 of the spam and in 40 of the ham. What is the probability that a random email from the 1,000 contains “free”? Give a fraction.

slips.say: That is only the spam with “free” ($120/1000$). Add the 40 ham.
That is $120/200$, the share of spam. Divide by 1,000, the number of all emails.

hints: Count all emails with the word, spam and ham together.

blocks.title: Spam and free together
blocks.why: "And" means both events at once. It is the first piece of the fraction in the definition.
blocks.prompt: Same table: 1,000 emails, 120 are spam containing “free”. What is $P(\text{spam and free})$ as a fraction of all 1,000?

slips.say: That is 120 out of the 200 spam. "Of all 1,000" means divide by 1,000.

hints: Only the emails that are both count.

blocks.title: Spam given free

define.meaning: $P(A \mid B)$, read “probability of $A$ given $B$”: among the cases where $B$ happened, the share where $A$ also happened. $P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \text{ and } B)}{P(B)}$.

blocks.why: This is what a spam filter actually needs: the email has the word, so how likely is spam?
blocks.prompt: 1,000 emails: 120 are spam with “free”, 40 are ham with “free”. $P(\text{spam and free}) = \frac{3}{25}$ and $P(\text{free}) = \frac{4}{25}$. Find $P(\text{spam} \mid \text{free})$ using $P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \text{ and } B)}{P(B)}$.

slips.say: That is the top of the fraction only. Divide by $P(\text{free})$.
That is the share of spam that has “free” ($120/200$), the other way round.
That is $P(\text{spam})$ with no condition. Given “free”, only the 160 emails with the word count.

hints: Look only at the emails with “free”. What share of them are spam?

check.say: Count: the denominator is the 160 emails with “free”.

blocks.solution: Learning that the email has “free” moves spam from $\frac15$ to $\frac34$.

blocks.title: Free given spam
blocks.why: The two directions sound alike and are different numbers. Mixing them up is the commonest slip in this subject.
blocks.prompt: Same table: 200 spam, 120 of them contain “free”. Find $P(\text{free} \mid \text{spam})$, the share of spam that contains “free”.

slips.say: That is $P(\text{spam} \mid \text{free})$, the share of “free” emails that are spam. Here the condition is spam, so divide by 200.

hints: Now only the spam emails count.

blocks.title: Which question is that?
blocks.why: Reading the condition correctly is the skill. The number follows.
blocks.prompt: Out of 1,000 emails, 200 are spam. 160 contain “free”, and 120 of those 160 are spam. What does $\frac{120}{160}$ answer?

options.text: Of the emails with “free”, what share are spam?
options.say: Right. The condition is “free”, so only the 160 count, and 120 of them are spam.

options.text: Of the spam emails, what share contain “free”?
options.say: Not this one. That is $\frac{120}{200}$: the condition is spam, so the base is the 200 spam.

options.text: Of all emails, what share are spam with “free”?
options.say: Not this one. That is $\frac{120}{1000}$: the base is all emails.

options.text: Of all emails, what share contain “free”?
options.say: Not this one. That is $\frac{160}{1000}$: the base is all emails.

blocks.hint: The number under the line is the group you look at. Which group is 160?
blocks.solution: The bottom number is always the condition's group: 160 emails with “free”.
